meta.hazardAnalysis:
Daily operations may take safety personnel to various locations which contain hazards with little or no time to return to the office to collect appropriate PPE. PPE must be taken with the employee and used when necessary, when conducting work outside the office.
- Foot hazards: PPE issued: Safety/steel-toe footwear
- Head hazards: PPE issued: Hard hat. Clean with mild soap and water.
- Hearing hazards: Personnel are not on a hearing conservation program but may enter areas where loud noise is present. Hearing protection (hard shell and disposable-type are provided in the work center. Clean hard shell earmuffs with mild soap and water.
- Hand hazards: PPE Issued: leather, nitrile, or mechanics-style gloves. Dispose of nitrile gloves in approved trash containers.
- Eye hazards: PPE issued: ANSI Z87.1 glasses. Clean with eye glass wipes. If contaminated with hazardous chemicals, dispose of them in approved containers and obtain a new pair from the supervisor.
- Nighttime/Reduced visibility traffic exposure: PPE Issued: Reflective vest and/or belt. Reflective vest or belt will be worn over the outer most garment when the employee is exposed to a traffic environment (i.e. roadways, flightline, etc.) during hours of darkness or reduced visibility.

meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
JBMDL Speed limit if not otheriwse posted = 25mph. Do not speed. Obey the rules of the road when responding to a mishap. Remember you are NOT a first responder and must obey all traffic rules and regulations.

Vehicle operators should pay their full attention to the operation of the vehicle. All drivers must follow applicable federal, state, local and host nation laws that are more stringent than this guidance on distractions while driving (e.g., using cellular phones, text messaging).

On base all traffic circles are one lane. Traffic entering the circle must yield to traffic in the circle.
When exiting the circle use your turn signals.

 Jug-handles are used extensively off base but not on base. No two jug-handles are the same. Be alert for other drivers who may cut you off trying to make their turn. If you miss your turn at a jughandle do not cut off other drivers. Instead, continue down the road until you can safely go back.

You can expect seasonal heavy fog, typically in Autumn. Reduce driving speeds and use your headlights.

New Jersey “Wipers On, Headlights On” Law
In New Jersey, you must have your headlights on whenever your windshield wipers are in use, regardless of whether it is day or night, and regardless of the amount of precipitation.

When Headlights Are Required
1) From half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise — even in clear weather.
2) Whenever you use your windshield wipers — this includes light drizzle, rain, snow, mist, or any other moisture that triggers wiper use.
3) When visibility drops below 500 feet due to fog, smoke, or other adverse conditions.

Passing on the Right in New Jersey. In New Jersey, passing on the right is generally prohibited unless specific safety conditions are met.

Passing on the Right is Permitted, only if:
1) The vehicle ahead is making or about to make a left turn and there is enough unobstructed pavement to do so safely.
2) The roadway has two or more substantially continuous lines of traffic moving in the same direction, allowing a lane change to the right.
3) On one-way streets, if the road is wide enough for two or more lines of traffic and free of obstructions.
4) In all these cases, you must pass at a safe distance to the left and not drive off the pavement or main-traveled portion of the road to complete the maneuver.

Passing on the right is illegal in most other situations, including:
1) When there is only one lane of traffic in the same direction.
2) When the vehicle ahead is not making a left turn.
3) When it is not safe to pass (e.g., hills, curves, intersections, railroad crossings, narrow bridges, or “No Passing” zones).
4) Anywhere on JBMDL unless the roadway has a left turn lane allowing the right lane to continue moving.

meta.medicalFacility:
The JB MDL Clinic does not provide emergency services. For any severe or life threatening injury call 911 for an ambulance.

Non-emergency:
1) During normal duty hours on weekdays (0800-1600), personnel should report to JB MDL Occupational Medicine Clinic (McGuire) for assessment and treatment of non-emergency injuries suffered while on-the-job. Civilian employees may elect to receive treatment from their personal physician.
2) If injuries are non-life threatening injuries, or injuries suffered during other than normal duty hours, go to the emergency room at Deborah (Browns Mills).

Emergency Medical Facilities.
1) Deborah Heart and Lung Center; 20 Pine Mill Road, Brown Mills, NJ 08015 (609) 283-9019.

meta.weatherShelter:
New Jersey tornadoes are rare, but possible. In the event of a tornado warning seek shelter in an interior romm on the lowest floor. If in a vehicle, park and exit the vehicle. Seek shelter in the lowest place available.

Lighting: Seek shelter indoors or inside and enclosed vehicle.

High temperatures during summer months. Drink plenty of fluids. Be aware of symptoms of heat exhaustion: skin is clammy and moist, fatigue, giddiness, nausea, and headache. If you or a coworker experience any of these symptoms the victim should rest in a cool place and drinkwater or an electrolyte solution. 

Heat stroke: body stops sweating, mental confusion, delirium, loss of consciousness, convulsions or coma, body temp of 106 degrees or higher, hot dry skin which may bered, mottled, or bluish. Seek medical attention at once. 

During the winter months it can get quite cold and you should always wear the proper clothes. It is your responsibility to ensure you have the right foul weather gear at work. 

South New Jersey has a very large pine forest. There is a year-round fire danger. If you smoke, be very mindful of where you smoke and how you dispose of your smoking materials.

selectedModules.title: Manual Lifting and Material Handling
selectedModules.reference: Manual lifting techniques and available lifting devices
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Cover shop-specific lifting limits, two-person lift triggers, hand truck and lifting-device use, and when supervisors require assisted handling. No direct OSHA 2254 standalone manual-lifting module is mapped here.
selectedModules.trainingSource: No direct OSHA 2254 - Training Requirements in OSHA Standards training excerpt; local procedures
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Supervisors must ensure thorough training on proper manual lifting techniques, required PPE, and the use of manual lifting devices. Training must use both verbal and written materials, include practice on proper motions, and be documented under DAFI 91-202.
selectedModules.afTrainingSource: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards para. 2.10.3
selectedModules.notes:
Back injuries are a significant cause of disability, with 75% of workplace-related back injuries occurring during lifting tasks. Following these guidelines can help minimize the risk of strains, sprains, fractures, and other injuries. 

Preparing for the Lift. Before you even touch the object, it is crucial to plan ahead. 
- Assess the Load. Test the weight ofthe object to ensure it is manageable. If it is too heavy or bulky, get assistance from a coworker or usemechanical aids like a dolly or hand truck. - Clear Your Path. Ensure the route you will take is free ofobstacles, debris, and is not slippery. Know where you will place the object before you lift it. - Warm-Up. Just like any other physical activity, it is important to warm up your muscles before lifting. Simplestretches for your back and legs can help prevent injuries. Proper Lifting Technique. The way you liftan object is critical to protecting your back and preventing injury. The goal is to use your legs, not yourback. - Get Close to the Load. Stand as close to the object as possible. The closer the load is to yourspine, the less force it exerts on your back. - Maintain a Stable Stance. Keep your feet shoulder-widthapart, with one foot slightly in front of the other for better balance. - Bend at Your Knees and Hips.Squat down by bending your hips and knees, keeping your back straight. Avoid bending forward. -Keep Your Back Straight. Maintain the natural curve of your lower back. Look straight ahead and keepyour shoulders back. - Grip the Load Securely. Get a firm grip on the object before lifting. - Lift withYour Legs. Straighten your legs to lift the object, keeping your back straight. Avoid jerking or snatchingthe load. - Keep the Load Close. Hold the object close to your body, at about waist level. Carrying andSetting Down the Load. The process of carrying and setting down the object is just as important asthe lift itself. - Avoid Twisting. Use your feet to change direction, taking small steps. Do not twist your
body while holding a heavy object. - Maintain Clear Vision. Make sure you can see over or around theload you are carrying. - Set Down Safely. To set the object down, reverse the lifting process. Squatdown by bending your knees and hips, keeping the load close to your body and your back straight.When to Use Mechanical Aids. For heavy, bulky lifting tasks, always consider using hand trucks. Byfollowing these ergonomic principles, you can significantly reduce your risk of injury when lifting andmoving objects. Remember, no single technique is perfect for every situation, so it is important toadapt these principles to the specific task at hand.

selectedModules.title: Slips, Trips, Falls
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Document the local task or hazard, identify where the training is located, and explain how completion is documented.
selectedModules.notes: Water may puddle around doors and walking surfaces during periods of heavy rainfall. This often causes the tile just inside the building doors to become wet. - Do use handrails. -Do watch where you are walking. - Do use extreme caution when entering and exiting the building. The wet tiles cause your boots to be slippery when you step onto the floor at once inside the building. - Do not carry items stacked above eye level up or down stairs. - Do not read or text while going up ordown stairs. - If wearing cleats in the winter remove them upon entering buildings.

selectedModules.title: Bloodborne Pathogens
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train exposed employees at initial assignment and at least annually, with additional training when tasks or procedures create new exposure. Cover disease signs and transmission, the exposure control plan, task recognition, engineering controls, work practices, PPE use and disposal, and Hepatitis B vaccine information.
selectedModules.trainingSource: OSHA 2254 - Training Requirements in OSHA Standards / 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Any person whose duties involve reasonably anticipated exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material must be trained and enrolled in the Bloodborne Pathogen Program. Supervisors of affected workplaces must establish a written exposure control plan and conduct training.
selectedModules.afTrainingSource: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards para. 1.9
selectedModules.notes: Your job does not typically require you to handle contaminated materials. If you are exposed to another person’s blood or other bodily substances, immediately clean the affected body part(s) with warm soapy water,  let your supervisor know and report to the occupational medicine clinic at the 87 MDG.

selectedModules.title: Airfield Driving
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Document the local task or hazard, identify where the training is located, and explain how completion is documented.
selectedModules.notes: The airfield/flightline is a hazardous environment. DO NOT operate any vehicle on the airfield/flightline unless you are licensed to do so. Always wear your reflective vest/belt when onthe airfield/flightline in reduced visibility. Be mindful of vehicles and aircraft movement. Aircraft have the right-of-way.

selectedModules.title: Unexploded Ordnance
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Document the local task or hazard, identify where the training is located, and explain how completion is documented.
selectedModules.notes:
The Dix ranges have been in use for one hundred years. There are UXOs on the ranges and on some areas of Lakehurst. DO NOT go down range on any range without first checking in with Range Control. 

RECOGNIZE, RETREAT, REPORT. Recognize the potential UXO, Retreat to a safe location, and Report it to SFS.

selectedModules.title: Tick-borne Illness
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Document the local task or hazard, identify where the training is located, and explain how completion is documented.
selectedModules.notes: New Jersey has an abundance of ticks and they can be found outdoors and indoors. Deer ticks may carry Lyme Disease. If you are bitten by a tick at work, first carefully remove the tick being careful not to break its jaws off as you remove it. Keep the tick and notify your supervisor. You can take the tick to the public health clinic at the 87 MDG where they may be able to test the tick for Lyme Disease. Keep an eye on the bite site for several days. If you see a rash or bulls-eye shaped mark notify your doctor and your supervisor. Alpha-gal syndrome is a food allergy to red meat and other products made from mammals. A Lone Star tick bite can transmits a sugar molecule called alpha-gal into the person’s body. This can trigger an immune system reaction that produces mild to severe allergic reactions to red meat.

selectedModules.afTrainingSource: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards Chapter 2
selectedModules.notes:
Complete the Office Safety course (RVCT-1070) on RedVector. 

Course Description: While we most often associate workplace injuries with construction, mining, manufacturing, and other manual labor jobs, injuries can occur even if you spend most of your workday sitting at a desk. Therefore, recognizing common hazards in an office environment and knowing how to reduce risks is vital to creating a safer workplace. This course discusses the common hazards in an office environment and how to reduce risks in order to help create a safer workplace.

Learning Objective: List some of the most common hazards and injuries in offices •Identify measures to prevent slips, trips, and falls •List ergonomic risk factors associated with office work and describe how to reduce the risk of musculoskeletal discomfort •Describe proper lifting technique •Describe how to prevent office fires •Describe the purpose and content of an emergency action plan
